findings.body:
Removing `@require_role("admin")` drops the only access control on `DELETE /users/<user>`. Any client that can reach this route can delete any user and get `204`, including accounts that cleanup jobs were never meant to touch.

Failure mode: a viewer (or unauthenticated caller, given no other auth middleware in `app.py`) sends `DELETE /users/alice` and removes the admin account from `USERS`.

Restore the decorator (or an equivalent admin/service-role check on the caller). If cleanup jobs need delete rights, grant them an explicit privileged identity — do not leave the endpoint open.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change removes the only authorization check on `DELETE /users/<user>`, leaving user deletion unauthenticated and unrestricted.

## Narrative

`delete_user` previously required `@require_role("admin")`. The PR replaces that decorator with a comment explaining that cleanup jobs running as the viewer account got 403s. After this change, any client that can reach the route can remove any entry from `USERS` and receive `204`.

That matches broken access control on a destructive endpoint: the failure mode is not limited to cleanup jobs; it is open deletion for every caller.

The 403s on viewer-account cleanup jobs are expected under an admin-only policy. The durable fix is to authenticate the job identity and authorize it explicitly (dedicated service role, admin credentials, or a separate internal cleanup path with its own guard) while keeping human/user-facing delete admin-protected.

Note while reviewing: `require_role` compares `ROLES.get(user)` where `user` is the path parameter (the account being deleted), not an authenticated caller from `request`. That design is itself questionable and may be why non-admin target deletes 403 — but removing the guard entirely is a regression, not a repair.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The patch removes `@require_role("admin")` from `DELETE /users/<user>`, leaving `delete_user` with no auth check and no other middleware in `app.py`, so any client can delete any user. Base still had the decorator; this is a real critical access-control regression.
